See also: monstré

English

[edit]

Noun

[edit]

monstre (plural monstres)

  1. Obsolete form of monster.

Anagrams

[edit]
  • Monters, mentors, meronts, metrons, monster, montres, termons

Catalan

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): (Central, Balearic) [ˈmɔns.tɾə]
  • IPA(key): (Valencia) [ˈmɔns.tɾe]
  • Audio (Barcelona):(file)

Noun

[edit]

monstre m (plural monstres)

  1. monster

Derived terms

[edit]
  • monstre de Gila

French

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

Inherited from Middle French monstre, from Old French monstre, borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /mɔ̃stʁ/
  • Audio:(file)
  • Audio (France (Toulouse)):(file)
  • Audio (France (Vosges)):(file)
  • Audio (France (Lyon)):(file)
  • Audio (France (Vosges)):(file)
  • Audio (France (Lyon)):(file)
  • Rhymes: -ɔ̃stʁ

Noun

[edit]

monstre m (plural monstres)

  1. monster
    Mon petit frère croit que des monstres habitent sous son lit.
    My little brother believes that monsters live under his bed.
  2. (figurative) hideous person, fiend

Derived terms

[edit]
  • monstrueux, monstrueuse
  • monstrueusement
  • monstre sacré

Related terms

[edit]
  • montrer

Descendants

[edit]
  • Haitian Creole: mons
  • → Romanian: monstru
  • → Russian: монстр (monstr)

Adjective

[edit]

monstre (plural monstres)

  1. (colloquial) enormous

Further reading

[edit]
  • “monstre”, in Trésor de la langue française informatisé [Digitized Treasury of the French Language], 2012

Anagrams

[edit]
  • mentors, montres, montrés

Italian

[edit]

Adjective

[edit]

monstre (invariable)

  1. extraordinary, exceptional
  2. monstrous (very large)

Middle English

[edit]

Alternative forms

[edit]
  • moustre (from Old French mostre etc.)

Etymology

[edit]

Borrowed from Old French monstre, borrowed itself from Latin monstrum.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈmɔnstər/, /ˈmɔnstrə/

Noun

[edit]

monstre (plural monstres)

  1. A monster or beast; a horrific or frightening creature.
  2. A marvelous or portentous occasion; a strange happening.
  3. (rare) Fate, luck; fortuitousness (as an allegorical figure)

Related terms

[edit]
  • monstruous

Descendants

[edit]
  • English: monster
  • Scots: monster

References

[edit]
  • “monstre, n.”, in MED Online, Ann Arbor, Mich.: University of Michigan, 2007, retrieved 3 October 2018.

Middle French

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From Old French monstre.

Noun

[edit]

monstre m (plural monstres)

  1. monster
    • 1542, Clement Marot, Oeuvres augmentees d'ung grand nombre de ses compositions nouvelles, link:
      Vien à l'umbrage en ce boys de grand' monstre
      Came into the shadow in these woods of a great monster

Descendants

[edit]
  • French: monstre
    • Haitian Creole: mons
    • → Romanian: monstru
    • → Russian: монстр (monstr)

Norman

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From Old French monstre, borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.

Noun

[edit]

monstre m (plural monstres)

  1. (Jersey) monster

Synonyms

[edit]
  • divèrs

Old French

[edit]

Alternative forms

[edit]
  • mostre, moustre

Etymology

[edit]

Borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.

Noun

[edit]

monstre oblique singular, m (oblique plural monstres, nominative singular monstres, nominative plural monstre)

  1. monster

Descendants

[edit]
  • Middle French: monstre
    • French: monstre
      • Haitian Creole: mons
      • → Romanian: monstru
      • → Russian: монстр (monstr)
  • Norman: monstre
  • → Middle Dutch: monster
    • Dutch: monster
  • → Middle English: monstre, moustre
    • English: monster
    • Scots: monster
